item.title: Efficiently Convert Integers to Hexadecimal Strings in Assembly & SIMD
item.description:
“Efficiently Convert Integers to Hexadecimal Strings in Assembly & SIMD”

Converting integers to their hexadecimal string representations is a common task in programming, often requiring efficient implementations for performance-critical applications. This involves processing each 4-bit segment (nibble) of an integer and mapping it to its corresponding ASCII hexadecimal character. Several approaches exist, ranging from traditional assembly loops to leveraging modern SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) extensions for parallel processing.

Core Logic: Nibble Extraction and Mapping

The fundamental principle behind integer-to-hexadecimal conversion is extracting each nibble (4 bits) of the integer and converting it into an ASCII character. Since hexadecimal is base-16, each digit represents 4 bits.

“Fixing C/C++ Inline Assembly Stack Corruption Issues with x86-64 ABI”

When integrating assembly code directly within C or C++ using GNU inline assembly, severe debugging challenges arise, often manifesting as unexpected program termination due to stack corruption. A primary culprit in x86-64 environments, particularly when compiling with default settings like -O0, is the misuse or violation of the stack pointer (%rsp) relative to the x86-64 System V Application Binary Interface (ABI).

item.title: x86 LEA Instruction: Beyond Address Calculation
item.description:
x86 LEA Instruction: Beyond Address Calculation

The x86 LEA (Load Effective Address) instruction, while its name suggests memory operations, possesses a surprisingly broad utility extending far beyond simply fetching memory addresses. It’s a powerful tool for arithmetic and register manipulation that, when leveraged correctly, can significantly streamline assembly code. But what exactly makes LEA so versatile, and how can we effectively employ it?

What is the Core Functionality of the LEA Instruction?

At its heart, LEA calculates an “effective address” based on a memory operand and stores this calculated address in a designated register. Crucially, it does not actually access memory at the calculated address. This non-destructive nature, coupled with its ability to perform complex address calculations in a single instruction, makes it a valuable asset for arithmetic operations.

item.title: Diving Deep into ARM Register Roles: FP, LR, SP, and PC
item.description:
“Diving Deep into ARM Register Roles: FP, LR, SP, and PC”

How do the Application Binary Interface (ABI) standards, specifically APCS versus the newer AAPCS (post-GCC 5.0+), dictate the usage of the Frame Pointer ($\text{FP}$) register in ARM architecture, particularly concerning stack tracing and unwinding?

The requirement for the Frame Pointer ($\text{FP}$) depends on the specific ABI standard in place. In the older APCS standard, $\text{FP}$ was mandated. However, under the modern AAPCS (as used by GCC 5.0 and later), utilizing $\text{FP}$ is optional. Even when not strictly required by the AAPCS, the compiler can still employ it. When $\text{FP}$ is used, debug information annotates the stack and frame pointer usage, aiding stack tracing and code unwinding. It is worth noting that if a function is compiled as static, the compiler has greater latitude and might not strictly adhere to any published convention.

“Assembly: Convert Binary Integers to Decimal ASCII Strings”

Converting a binary integer to its decimal ASCII string representation in assembly involves a series of arithmetic operations and character manipulations. The core idea is to repeatedly extract the least significant digit of the number and convert it into its corresponding ASCII character. This process is typically done by dividing the number by 10, using the remainder to get the digit, and then converting that digit to its ASCII representation.

item.title: Fixing SIGSEGV: 16-Byte Stack Alignment Issues in x86-64 Assembly
item.description:
“Fixing SIGSEGV: 16-Byte Stack Alignment Issues in x86-64 Assembly”

Encountering a SIGSEGV (Segmentation Fault) can be a cryptic hurdle in low-level programming. One frequent culprit, particularly in x86-64 architecture when interacting with modern C library functions like printf or scanf, is insufficient stack alignment. This post delves into the reasons behind this requirement and provides actionable solutions.

The x86-64 System V ABI (Application Binary Interface) mandates a 16-byte stack alignment for function calls. This means that before a function makes another call, the stack pointer (RSP) must be a multiple of 16. Why this strictness? Modern compilers, like GCC, increasingly leverage advanced instruction sets such as SSE2 for performance. Instructions like movaps (move aligned packed single-precision floats) require their operands, including memory locations on the stack, to be 16-byte aligned. Failure to meet this alignment results in a SIGSEGV.
